facts.claim: Bourbon Restoration; Senegal returned to France by the treaties; convoy from Rochefort in June 1816 led by the frigate Méduse; about 400 aboard incl. the new governor
Captain Hugues Duroy de Chaumareys, royalist émigré, had hardly sailed in 20 years; appointed reportedly for nobility/royalism
He lost contact with the other ships and let a passenger with no qualifications (Richefort) help navigate; about 160 km off course
Ran aground 2 July 1816 on the Arguin Bank off present-day Mauritania
Six boats; raft built from masts and spars, about 20 m long; 5 July 1816: about 146 men and one woman
Supplies: a bag of biscuit eaten on day one, two casks of water lost, six casks of wine; 17 men stayed on the ship
Captain left before all passengers were off (court-martial finding)
After only a few miles the raft was turned loose/the lines cut; rudderless
First night ~20 men lost; quote 'This whole night we contended against death' (Savigny & Corréard, 1818 English translation)
Drunken revolt against the officers with sabre and boarding-axe; many killed
By the fourth day 67 alive; flying fish caught; cannibalism; quote 'Those whom death had spared in the disastrous night ... fell upon the dead bodies'
Eighth day: the fittest threw the weak and wounded overboard, leaving 15
17 July 1816: the Argus found the raft by chance after 13 days; it disappeared and reappeared about two hours later; 15 alive; 5 died soon after; 3 of the 17 on the wreck survived
News reached Paris in September 1816; Savigny's report leaked to the anti-government Journal des débats (13 Sept 1816)
Court-martial at Rochefort 1817: guilty of incompetent navigation and abandoning the ship before all passengers were off; could have faced death; 3 years in prison
Savigny & Corréard's book (1817) became a bestseller, translated into several languages
Géricault (b. 26 Sep 1791) had broken off an affair with his aunt; shaved his head; near-monastic life in his studio Nov 1818-July 1819 (Faubourg du Roule)
He met Savigny and Corréard; scale model of the raft with them and the carpenter Lavillette
Morgue of the Hôpital Beaujon; severed limbs in the studio; one account: a severed head from an asylum on his studio roof for a fortnight
Studies of severed heads (Nationalmuseum Stockholm) and anatomical pieces (Musée Fabre, Montpellier)
Delacroix posed for the foreground (face-down) figure; Savigny and Corréard painted from life; assistant Louis-Alexis Jamar posed for the dead youth
More than 100 studies; he considered the mutiny, cannibalism and rescue before the sighting of the Argus
The moment: first sight of the Argus on the horizon; Jean Charles waving a handkerchief from an empty barrel; Jean Charles died soon after the rescue; model Joseph, of Haitian descent
Pyramidal composition; the old man with the dead youth recalls Dante's Ugolino
Canvas 491 × 716 cm

Salon of 1819 as 'Scène de naufrage'; critics divided ('pile of corpses'); Louis XVIII reportedly: 'your shipwreck is certainly no disaster'; gold medal, not bought by the state; Delacroix deeply affected
London 1820, Bullock's Egyptian Hall, Piccadilly: about 40,000 visitors; nearly 20,000 francs (LRB: more than 17,000)
Géricault died in Paris 26 January 1824, aged 32, weakened by riding accidents and tubercular infection
The Louvre (Comte de Forbin) bought the painting from his heirs in 1824
Bitumen has darkened and wrinkled the surface irreversibly; large areas hard to see

youtube.description_lead: In July 1816 the French frigate Méduse ran aground off West Africa. A hundred and forty-seven people were put on a raft and cut loose. Thirteen days later, fifteen were alive. Two years later, a 26-year-old painter shaved his head, locked himself in his studio with the dead, and turned the scandal into one of the most famous paintings in the Louvre. This is the true story of Théodore Géricault's Raft of the Medusa.
